title: Moving to Las Vegas: where to live across the valley
summary: The valley is five or six different places wearing one name. How to tell them apart before you sign a lease, and where Lugg's data says people land.
body_markdown:
Moving to Las Vegas is a choice between five or six distinct parts of one valley, and they feel almost nothing alike. The metro has added[more than 140,000 people since 2020](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-total-metro-and-micro-statistical-areas.html) , and roughly six in seven of that growth came from people moving in rather than being born here, according to the Census Bureau's 2025 population estimates.


At Lugg, more than four in five local moves inside the valley since the start of 2026 started and ended in the same city, so the part you land in tends to be the part you stay in. Lugg is an on-demand moving and delivery service that moves furniture and whole apartments between neighborhoods across the Las Vegas valley, with movers and a truck on the way within the hour for anything too big to fit in a car.


## The valley at a glance


Area What it is Who it tends to suit


Summerlin Master-planned, on the western edge against Red Rock. Parks, trails, Downtown Summerlin retail Buyers with the budget for the valley's premium suburb


Henderson Southeastern suburb, Nevada's second-largest city on its own Families prioritizing schools and predictability


Southwest / Enterprise The valley's newest construction, between the Strip and the southern edge People who want a newer place and more square footage


North Las Vegas Northern end, historically the most affordable First-time buyers and renters stretching a budget


Downtown / Arts District The urban core, north of the Strip Renters who want to walk somewhere


Boulder City Small, separate, out toward the lake People who want out of the metro entirely


## Which parts of the valley are actually Las Vegas?


The city of Las Vegas is really just downtown and the neighborhoods around it. Almost everything else people call Las Vegas is Clark County, and the clearest case is the Strip, which isn't in the city at all. Most of it sits in Paradise, with the north end in Winchester. The arrangement dates to 1950, when the city tried to annex the casinos and the casinos lobbied the county to let them become their own towns instead.


Paradise, Spring Valley, Enterprise and Sunrise Manor are all[unincorporated towns run by Clark County](https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/departments/comprehensive_planning_department/divisions/advanced_planning_division/spring-valley) . Henderson, North Las Vegas and Boulder City are separate cities with their own governments. The mail hides all of it, because those ZIP codes carry a Las Vegas address either way. It matters when you're comparing listings, since a site putting Henderson side by side with "Las Vegas" isn't comparing like with like, and it matters again once you've moved, because it decides which government handles your permits and your trash pickup.


## What are the best neighborhoods in Las Vegas?


There's no single best neighborhood in Las Vegas, and the choice comes down to three things: your commute tolerance, whether schools are a hard requirement, and your budget ceiling.


**Commute** is the factor people get wrong. The valley's biggest employment cluster is the Strip, which sits in Paradise next to the airport, near the middle of the metro. From either Summerlin or Henderson that's a comparable drive, so for a Strip job the suburb you pick is a lifestyle and price decision.


**Schools** work differently here than in most metros, because Nevada organizes school districts by county. Clark County School District covers the entire valley, Henderson, North Las Vegas and Boulder City included, so "moving to Henderson for the schools" really means moving into one particular school's zone. Check the zone, because the district is the same valley-wide.


**Budget** runs in a rough order:[North Las Vegas](https://lugg.com/cities/nv/north-las-vegas) , then the southwest around Enterprise, then Henderson, then[Summerlin](https://lugg.com/cities/nv/summerlin) at the top of the market. The spread is real money: over the three months to July 2026 the median home sold for[$425,000 in North Las Vegas](https://www.redfin.com/city/13363/NV/North-Las-Vegas/housing-market) and[$645,000 in Summerlin](https://www.redfin.com/neighborhood/767374/NV/Las-Vegas/Summerlin/housing-market) . Inside Summerlin the newer southern villages cost more than the older northern ones, so it's worth looking at the older northern villages before you write the area off on price.


**The southwest** , including the unincorporated town of Enterprise, is where a lot of the valley's newer housing has gone. If you want a house built this decade without Summerlin pricing, this is usually the answer. Keep west on Blue Diamond and the subdivisions run out into open desert. Cactus Joe's nursery is out that way, and a yard here is a different project from the one you left: gravel, drip line and desert plants where you're used to grass, and most new builds come landscaped that way already.


**North Las Vegas** is where the gap between one neighborhood and the next is widest, so it rewards driving around before you sign anything.


**Downtown and the Arts District** are the only part of the valley where you can reasonably live without a car being central to your day, and the only part of it that sits inside the actual city of Las Vegas. The housing stock is older and more mixed than anywhere else in the metro, so what you get changes block to block.


## Henderson or Summerlin?


Pick Henderson if you want predictability, and Summerlin if you want the polished version and have the budget for it. The two have more in common than the comparison suggests: both are planned, and both are built around cars and cul-de-sacs.


The differences that matter day to day are geographic. Summerlin sits on the west side against the canyon, so you get the mountain views and a longer drive to the airport. Henderson is southeast, closer to the airport and to Lake Mead. If your job is on the west side or you hike on weekday mornings, Summerlin. If it's in the southeast industrial corridor, Henderson.


If you genuinely can't choose, rent in one for a year before you buy.


## What does it cost to live in Las Vegas?


The Las Vegas metro's median gross rent is **$1,739 a month** , its median home value is **$451,000** , and median household income is **$80,028** , on the Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey. Nevada charges no state income tax, so a given salary goes further here than it would in a state that taxes it.


Moving something inside the valley is cheap. Getting a single piece of furniture across town with one mover has cost a median of **$76** since Lugg launched in Las Vegas at the start of 2026. Lugg is an on-demand moving and delivery service that scales from that up to a full apartment, with no hourly minimums.


## Is Las Vegas a good place to live?


Las Vegas is a good place to live if you want a low-tax metro with serious outdoor access nearby, and a difficult one if you struggle with heat. The valley is home to about 2.4 million people, and Red Rock and Lake Mead are both close enough for an ordinary Saturday.


The honest counterweight is the economy. Tourism, gaming and hospitality anchor it, so a lot of the work here depends on how many people are visiting, and downturns land harder here than in metros with a broader employment base.


## What is living in Las Vegas actually like day to day?


Living in Las Vegas is a car-dependent life with shorter drives than the map suggests. The urban area covers roughly 540 square miles and the 215 Beltway loops most of it, so most trips run well under half an hour. Summerlin to Henderson is a real drive across the whole metro, which surprises people who think of both as Las Vegas.


Heat organizes the calendar from about May to September. Errands move to early morning, patios empty out in the afternoon, and a pool becomes a practical feature to shop for. Summer is long, and it isn't something you acclimate to in one season.


## How do you move between Las Vegas neighborhoods?


Moving between valley neighborhoods usually comes down to one decision: vehicle size. A studio or a few pieces of furniture generally fits a cargo van or a Sprinter; a full house needs a box truck. You pick the vehicle when you book, so it's worth measuring the largest thing you own before you choose.


Most valley moves are short. Across Lugg's Las Vegas moves so far this year, the median household move has covered about **four miles** . Las Vegas is also the one city in[Lugg's analysis of local moving costs across 22 U.S. cities](https://lugg.com/blog/local-moving-cost-by-city) where the mattress, rather than the couch, tops the most-moved-item list, and its busiest moving day is Friday instead of the Saturday that dominates almost everywhere else. One Lugg can cross city lines inside the valley, so a[furniture move inside Las Vegas](https://lugg.com/las-vegas-nv-furniture-movers) and a move into[Henderson](https://lugg.com/cities/nv/henderson) are the same job. Movers carry items up stairs, into elevators and down the long hallways that valley apartment complexes specialize in, and your move is fully backed by the Damage Protection Guarantee, up to $10,000 on eligible claims.


Three things worth planning around here:


- Book the early morning slot between May and September. A closed truck box sitting in a valley summer gets far hotter than the air outside, which is worth knowing if you're moving candles, electronics or anything with a screen.
- Many of the planned communities in Summerlin and Henderson are gated, so the crew will need the gate code or a call ahead to the guardhouse.
- A lot of the valley's newer townhomes put the garage at street level and the living space a floor or two up, so plan for everything going up[two flights](https://lugg.com/blog/how-to-move-a-couch) .


## Picking your part of the valley


The differences between these areas are bigger than they look from outside the valley. Drive all of them on a weekday at rush hour before you decide, and again on a Saturday morning.


When you've picked your part of the valley, book[movers in Las Vegas](https://lugg.com/cities/nv/las-vegas) through Lugg. Movers are on the way within the hour, or you pick the one-hour window that suits you, which is how most people here get a load done before the afternoon heat.
